title: Develop event-driven AI workflows with Azure Event Grid

questions.q: New documents arrive in Blob Storage, and an embeddings pipeline currently polls the container every five minutes. What should replace the polling?

options.text: A custom topic
options.why: The pipeline consumes this event; Blob Storage publishes it through a system topic.

options.text: A Service Bus queue polled each minute
options.why: That's still polling.

options.text: A webhook that lists the container
options.why: Listing on a timer is still polling.

options.text: An Event Grid subscription to BlobCreated
options.why: Correct. The system topic pushes a BlobCreated event as soon as the blob appears.

questions.hint: Stop asking the container whether something is new. Let the platform tell you.
questions.explain: Reactive data processing: subscribe to storage events instead of polling.

questions.q: Which statement about Event Grid system topics is true?

options.text: You publish your application's events to them
options.why: Only the Azure service publishes to a system topic.

options.text: They support pull delivery and nothing else
options.why: Learn doesn't limit system topics to pull delivery.

options.text: They're created automatically for Azure services
options.why: Correct. They appear when you subscribe to a supported Azure resource's events.

options.text: They require you to define the event schema
options.why: System topic schemas are predefined by the service.

questions.hint: Azure services publish through topics that Event Grid creates for them.
questions.explain: System topics: Azure services. Custom topics: your code.

questions.q: Match each requirement to the event handler Learn describes.

items.text: Lightweight, stateless processing with automatic scaling
Feed events into a high-throughput streaming pipeline

items.why: Service Bus suits guaranteed ordering or transactions.

items.text: Send events to a custom inference endpoint over HTTP

questions.hint: Match each processing need to the handler built for it.
questions.explain: Choose the handler by processing requirements.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A content moderation platform uses Event Grid.

rows.text: Uploads trigger Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated events from a system topic.
rows.why: Blob Storage publishes through a system topic.

rows.text: The classifier can publish com.contoso.ai.ContentClassified to the same system topic.
rows.why: You can't publish to system topics; use a custom topic.

rows.text: Notification and analytics services can each subscribe to the custom topic independently.
Each event should carry the full uploaded image.
rows.why: Events are lightweight notifications; subscribers fetch the resource.

questions.hint: Azure events come through system topics. Your own events go to custom topics.
questions.explain: System topics for Azure events, custom topics for your own; keep events small.

questions.q: A consumer can't accept incoming HTTP requests and wants to read events at its own pace. Which option fits?

options.text: A system topic with a webhook
options.why: Webhooks are push delivery.

options.text: Pull delivery from a namespace topic
options.why: Correct. Namespace topics support pull delivery, so the consumer reads on demand.

options.text: Push delivery to a webhook endpoint it hosts
options.why: Webhooks need an HTTP endpoint that accepts requests.

options.text: A custom topic with push delivery to Functions
options.why: That's push delivery.

questions.hint: If the consumer can't receive HTTP, it has to go and fetch events.
questions.explain: Push sends to an endpoint; pull lets the consumer connect and read.

questions.q: A team is designing a new set of AI pipeline events and must choose an event schema. They want an open, protocol-independent standard that works beyond Azure. Which schema does Learn recommend?

options.text: Event Grid schema
options.why: The Event Grid schema remains for backward compatibility. It's not the recommendation for new work.

options.text: Event Hubs Avro
options.why: Avro is a serialization format, not an Event Grid event schema.

options.text: Custom JSON with no required attributes
options.why: Without standard attributes, subscribers can't rely on id, source or type.

options.text: CloudEvents v1.0
options.why: Correct. CloudEvents v1.0 is an open CNCF standard and the recommended schema for new implementations.

questions.hint: One schema is an open standard from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.
questions.explain: CloudEvents v1.0 is recommended for new implementations: an open, protocol-independent CNCF standard. The Event Grid schema is kept for backward compatibility and can't represent CloudEvents extension attributes.

questions.q: Which CloudEvents attribute should subscribers use to detect and deduplicate repeated deliveries?

options.text: The id attribute of each event
options.why: Correct. id uniquely identifies each event.

options.text: type attribute
options.why: type categorizes the event.

options.text: subject attribute
options.why: subject is a filterable path.

options.text: source attribute
options.why: source identifies the originating system.

questions.hint: Event Grid may deliver the same event more than once. Which attribute is unique per event?
questions.explain: Event Grid is at-least-once, so handlers dedupe on id.

questions.q: A subscription should receive only events from the embeddings pipeline, whose subjects look like `/pipelines/embeddings/batch-42`. Which filter fits?

options.text: --included-event-types /pipelines/embeddings
options.why: Event types aren't subject paths.

options.text: subjectEndsWith /embeddings
options.why: The subject doesn't end with /embeddings.

options.text: StringContains on the id attribute
options.why: id is a unique identifier, not a routing path.

options.text: subjectBeginsWith /pipelines/embeddings/
options.why: Correct. A prefix filter routes events from a specific pipeline.

questions.hint: The subjects share a prefix. Filter on how the subject starts.
questions.explain: Set hierarchical subjects so subscribers can filter by prefix or suffix.

questions.q: Your topic publishes CloudEvents, and a legacy handler only accepts the Event Grid schema. What happens if you set the subscription's delivery schema to the Event Grid schema?

options.text: Event Grid converts it, dropping extension attributes
options.why: Learn says this conversion isn't supported at all.

options.text: That conversion isn't supported for CloudEvents topics
options.why: Correct. CloudEvents-to-Event Grid conversion isn't supported because of extension attributes.

options.text: The topic switches its input schema automatically
options.why: Input schema is set on the topic and doesn't change automatically.

options.text: Both formats arrive in one payload
options.why: Event Grid doesn't do this.

questions.hint: Conversion works in one direction only.
questions.explain: Event Grid schema → CloudEvents works; the reverse doesn't.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A subscription has two advanced filters: `data.status StringIn [flagged, failed]` and `data.confidence NumberGreaterThan 0.9`.

rows.text: An event with status flagged and confidence 0.95 is delivered.
rows.why: It meets both conditions (AND between conditions).

rows.text: An event with status failed and confidence 0.5 is delivered.
rows.why: Both conditions must match; 0.5 fails the second.

rows.text: An event with status failed and confidence 0.97 is delivered.
rows.why: Within a condition's values, OR applies: failed matches.

rows.text: A subscription can have up to 100 advanced filter conditions.
rows.why: The limit is 25 conditions per subscription.

questions.hint: Conditions combine with AND; values inside one condition combine with OR.
questions.explain: AND between conditions, OR within each condition's values.

questions.q: A review service should receive only InferenceCompleted events from the content-moderation pipeline. How do type and subject filters on one subscription combine?

options.text: An event has to match both of the filters
options.why: Correct. A subscription with both filters only receives events matching all criteria.

options.text: A subscription allows one filter type at most
options.why: You can combine type and subject filtering.

options.text: An event that matches either filter is delivered
options.why: Filters on the same subscription combine with AND.

options.text: The subject filter replaces the type filter
options.why: Both filters apply.

questions.hint: Type says what happened, and subject says where. How do two filters on one subscription combine?
questions.explain: Use type filtering for what happened and subject filtering for where.

questions.q: Only inference results with a confidence above 0.9 should reach the auto-approve handler. Confidence is a number in the event's data. Which subscription filter does this?

options.text: Event type filter: com.contoso.ai.HighConfidence
options.why: That only works if the publisher creates a separate event type, which it doesn't.

options.text: Subject filter: subjectEndsWith confidence-0.9
options.why: Subject filters match text in the subject, not numbers in the data.

options.text: Advanced filter: data.confidence NumberGreaterThan 0.9
options.why: Correct. Advanced filters compare values inside the event data.

options.text: Output batching with a preferred batch size of 0.9 KB
options.why: Batching groups deliveries. It doesn't filter events.

questions.hint: The value is a number inside data. Which filter type can compare numbers?
questions.explain: Advanced filters match on values in the event data, with operators such as NumberGreaterThan and StringIn. Type and subject filters don't evaluate numeric payload values.

questions.q: An inference handler takes about 2 minutes per event, and Event Grid keeps retrying events that were actually processed. What should the handler do?

options.text: Return 400 so Event Grid stops retrying
options.why: 400 means "don't retry" for a malformed request, not for success.

options.text: Increase Event Grid's timeout to 5 minutes
options.why: The 30-second wait isn't something you raise.

options.text: Return 202 Accepted at once, then process
options.why: Correct. 202 counts as successful delivery; Event Grid waits only 30 seconds.

options.text: Return 503 after the work is finished
options.why: 503 signals overload and triggers retries.

questions.hint: Event Grid waits only a short time. Acknowledge first, then do the slow work.
questions.explain: Acknowledge early with 202 when processing takes longer than 30 seconds.

questions.q: What is Event Grid's default maximum number of delivery attempts?

options.why: 1,440 is the default event TTL in minutes.
24 isn't the default.
Correct. Default max attempts is 30 (range 1–30).
10 is the Service Bus default max delivery count.

questions.hint: Default maximum delivery attempts is a round number.
questions.explain: Max attempts default 30; event TTL default 1,440 minutes (24 hours).

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An event subscription uses default settings and its webhook returns errors.

rows.text: If the webhook returns 400 Bad Request, Event Grid retries with backoff.
If it returns 503, Event Grid retries following its backoff schedule.
Events that exhaust retries are kept in Blob Storage automatically.
rows.why: Dead-lettering is disabled by default; without it, events are dropped.

rows.text: The handler might receive the same event twice.

questions.hint: Some status codes are retried and some aren't. Exhausted events aren't kept unless you enable it.
questions.explain: Return accurate status codes, make handlers idempotent and configure dead-lettering.

questions.q: A real-time moderation subscription should stop retrying stale events after 30 minutes. A teammate also sets max attempts to 10. What happens?

options.text: TTL wins first, after about six attempts
options.why: Correct. Whichever limit comes first stops retries; only about six attempts fit in 30 minutes.

options.text: All 10 attempts run, then it stops
options.why: The TTL expires before 10 attempts.

options.text: TTL is ignored once max attempts is set
options.why: Both limits apply.

options.text: Event Grid retries every 3 minutes to fit 10 attempts
options.why: The backoff schedule doesn't stretch to fit.

questions.hint: Two limits apply. Which one runs out sooner with the default retry schedule?
questions.explain: Retry stops at the first of max attempts or event TTL.

questions.q: Dead-lettered events show lastDeliveryOutcome = NotFound for all of them since yesterday's deployment. What's the most likely issue?

options.text: The handler endpoint URL changed
options.why: Correct. Learn ties a batch of NotFound outcomes to a changed handler URL.

options.text: The TTL is too long
options.why: TTL length doesn't produce NotFound.

options.text: The inference service is overloaded
options.why: Overload shows up as TimedOut or Busy.

options.text: Events are too large
options.why: 413 isn't a NotFound outcome.

questions.hint: NotFound for every event after a deployment points at the destination.
questions.explain: Use deadLetterReason and lastDeliveryOutcome to diagnose systemic failures.

questions.q: Which response from an event handler does Event Grid treat as a successful delivery?

options.text: 503 Service Unavailable
options.why: 503 tells Event Grid to retry. It isn't a success.

options.text: 202 Accepted
options.why: Correct. Event Grid treats 200, 201, 202, 203 and 204 as success.

options.text: 400 Bad Request
options.why: 400 is a permanent error. Event Grid doesn't retry it, and it isn't a success.

options.text: 413 Request Entity Too Large
options.why: 413 is a permanent error, not a success.

questions.hint: Success is in the 2xx range.
questions.explain: Event Grid treats 200–204 as successful delivery. 400 and 413 are permanent errors (not retried); 503 triggers retries with backoff.

questions.q: You enable dead-lettering on an event subscription so that undeliverable events are kept. Where does Event Grid write them?

options.text: To an Azure Storage queue
options.why: Event Grid dead-letters to Blob Storage, not Storage queues.

options.text: To a Log Analytics table
options.why: Logs can record delivery failures, but the events themselves go to Blob Storage.

options.text: To a Service Bus dead-letter queue created automatically
options.why: Event Grid doesn't use Service Bus for its dead-letter location.

options.text: To an Azure Blob Storage container that already exists
options.why: Correct. Dead-lettered events go to a Blob container you specify, which must exist beforehand.

questions.hint: Dead-lettering is off by default, and you must point it at existing storage.
questions.explain: Dead-lettering is off by default. When enabled, undeliverable events go to an Azure Blob Storage container you specify (it must exist). They carry properties such as deadLetterReason and lastDeliveryOutcome.

questions.q: A webhook handler returns 400 whenever its vector database is briefly unavailable, and those events are never processed. What's the right fix?

options.text: Enable output batching on the subscription
options.why: Batching groups events. It doesn't change how errors are retried.

options.text: Raise max delivery attempts from 10 to 30
options.why: More attempts don't help when the status code stops retries completely.

options.text: Return 503 during the outage so that Event Grid retries
options.why: Correct. 503 triggers retries with backoff, while 400 means a permanent problem and is never retried.

options.text: Return 401 so that Event Grid retries in five minutes
options.why: 401 isn't retried for webhook endpoints, so the events would still be lost.

questions.hint: The handler is telling Event Grid the event is bad, when really the database is down for a moment.
questions.explain: Return accurate status codes: 400 means a permanent payload problem and isn't retried; use 503 for temporary outages so Event Grid retries with exponential backoff. Make handlers idempotent.

questions.q: A subscription uses output batching with up to 100 events per delivery. The handler fails on one event in a batch. How does Event Grid respond?

options.text: It splits the batch in half and retries each half
options.why: Event Grid doesn't split batches on failure.

options.text: It retries the whole batch of 100 events
options.why: Correct. Batch delivery is all or nothing, so handlers must be idempotent.

options.text: It retries the failed event alone
options.why: Event Grid doesn't track success per event inside a batch.

options.text: It dead-letters only the failed event
options.why: Without per-event acknowledgment, it can't single out one event.

questions.hint: The handler acknowledges a batch with one response.
questions.explain: Output batching is all-or-none: if any event fails, Event Grid retries the whole batch. Keep handlers idempotent and batches small enough to finish within the 30-second timeout.

questions.q: A Container Apps service publishes custom events with a managed identity. Which role should the identity have on the custom topic?

options.text: Storage Blob Data Contributor
options.why: That's for Blob Storage.

options.text: Azure Service Bus Data Sender
options.why: That's for Service Bus.

options.text: Event Grid Contributor
options.why: Learn names Data Sender for publishing.

options.text: Event Grid Data Sender
options.why: Correct. Grant the managed identity Event Grid Data Sender on the topic.

questions.hint: Production publishers should use Entra ID, with the role that allows sending.
questions.explain: Entra ID with managed identity is the recommended production auth.

questions.q: An inference result is a 3 MB JSON document. What should the InferenceCompleted event's data contain?

options.text: A link to the stored result plus a summary
options.why: Correct. Reference results, add metadata and a summary for fast decisions.

options.text: The full 3 MB result, so nothing is fetched
options.why: Don't embed full results in events.

options.text: The result split across several events
options.why: Splitting isn't the recommended design.

options.text: Nothing; subscribers query the model again
options.why: Subscribers shouldn't recompute results.

questions.hint: Events describe what happened and where to find the details.
questions.explain: Events describe what happened and where to find details.

questions.q: A CI/CD pipeline publishes a CloudEvent to a custom topic with curl. Which two settings does Learn show? (Select two.)

options.text: A Bearer token for `https://dynamicsessions.io`
options.why: That audience is for dynamic sessions, not Event Grid.

options.text: `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
options.why: Form encoding isn't used for CloudEvents.

options.text: An `aeg-sas-key` header with the topic key
options.why: Correct. Learn's REST example authenticates with aeg-sas-key.

options.text: `Content-Type: application/cloudevents+json; charset=utf-8`
options.why: Correct. That's the content type for a single CloudEvent.

questions.hint: One setting tells Event Grid the payload format. The other authenticates the request when you don't use Entra ID.
questions.explain: The REST API returns 200 OK when the event is accepted.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A pipeline publishes five StageCompleted events using EventGridPublisherClient.

rows.text: Passing a list of five CloudEvents sends them in one HTTP request.
rows.why: Batch publishing sends a list in a single request.

rows.text: Each event should include a pipeline run ID so subscribers can correlate stages.
The producer must know which subscribers will receive the events.
rows.why: Producers don't need to know who subscribes.

questions.hint: One request can carry several events. Correlation IDs tie the stages together.
questions.explain: Publish at natural checkpoints with correlation IDs; subscribers come and go independently.
